# Block 9: Functionalise a script step and prove the result is unchanged {.unnumbered} :::{.callout-note} **Last verified:** 9 October 2026, against the Claude Code permissions documentation (code.claude.com) and GitHub's documentation on customising the Copilot cloud agent's environment (docs.github.com). ::: You have a computation that already works and you want to turn it into a reusable function. An agent can do that in seconds. The hard part is not the refactor but the verification: a change that "improves" code can quietly alter its output, so how do you confirm the function still does what the script did? The method is to freeze the original result before anything is touched. You run the analysis once, save its output to a reference file (an `.rds`), and require the new function to reproduce that reference exactly. This is a *characterisation test*. It establishes that the output is **unchanged**, not that it is **correct**. Step 4 shows why that distinction matters, using a missing value that has been in the data all along. The block has a shared spine and three paths that differ in who writes the function and the test: - **Path A: by hand.** You write the function and the test. Slowest, and the path that teaches the verification logic most directly. Start here if testthat is new to you. - **Path B: a local agent, in two prompts.** Claude Code, Posit Assistant or Copilot in your IDE does the refactor and then the test, and you verify between them. - **Path C: an asynchronous agent.** You describe the work in GitHub issues; the Copilot cloud agent does it remotely and returns pull requests for you to review. All paths rejoin at Step 4. *⏱ ~60 minutes* ## The repository layout ``` repo/ ├── .claude/settings.json deny rules (Claude Code) ├── .github/ │ ├── CODEOWNERS your review required for protected paths │ └── workflows/ │ ├── r-checks.yml the independent check │ └── copilot-setup-steps.yml the cloud agent's environment ├── data/ │ └── raw/ │ └── voles_metabolism.csv contains one NA, on purpose ├── scripts/ │ ├── 01_load_data.R │ ├── 02_analysis.R │ └── functions/ │ ├── load_voles.R │ └── summary_functions.R created in this block ├── tests/ │ ├── make_reference.R run once, by you │ ├── fixtures/ │ │ └── metabolic_summary.rds the frozen reference │ └── test_summary_functions.R created in this block └── renv.lock pins tidyverse, here, testthat, renv ``` The single most important property of this layout: the file `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds` is created by you, once, and by nobody else. Every protection in this block exists to keep that true. ## The original scripts The data are read by one function that states every column type. The analysis, the reference and the test all call it, so they read the data identically. A column whose type `read_csv()` guesses differently in one place produces a test failure that has nothing to do with the refactor. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/load_voles.R ---- load_voles <- function() { readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), col_types = readr::cols( subject_id = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(), mass_post_g = readr::col_double(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double() ) ) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/01_load_data.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) voles <- load_voles() ``` ::: Inspect the data with `glimpse(voles)` at the console, not inside the script, so that sourcing the script from a test prints nothing. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/02_analysis.R: the original, trusted version ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "01_load_data.R")) metabolic_summary <- voles |> group_by(treatment_arm, sex) |> summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = n(), .groups = "drop" ) ``` ::: Two things to notice now and leave alone: 1. The data contain one missing value in `metabolic_rate_post`, and this code has no `na.rm`, so one cell of the result is `NA`. Do not "fix" it yet. Step 4 is about exactly this. 2. `group_by()` returns groups sorted by their keys. The `.by` argument returns them in order of first appearance in the data. If the two orders differ, a refactor that switches to `.by` changes the row order of the output. ## Step 0 (spine): capture and protect the reference Before anything else, run `scripts/02_analysis.R` yourself and confirm that `metabolic_summary` looks as you expect, including the one `NA` cell. Then run the capture script **once**: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/make_reference.R ---- # Run ONCE, by you, BEFORE any refactoring. source(here::here("scripts", "02_analysis.R")) dir.create(here::here("tests", "fixtures"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE) saveRDS( metabolic_summary, here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds") ) ``` ::: Commit the reference immediately, so that any later change to it is visible: ```bash git add tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds git commit -m "Capture reference output before refactoring" ``` Capture it now, before the refactor. Afterwards, `02_analysis.R` computes the summary through the very function under test, so re-capturing would compare the function with itself. **Protect it.** Each control covers a different route: - **Local agent (Claude Code).** Add deny rules to `.claude/settings.json`: ```json { "permissions": { "deny": [ "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)", "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)", "Edit(/data/**)", "Edit(/.github/**)" ] } } ``` Run `/permissions` to confirm the rules are active, then ask the agent to delete the `.rds` file and check that it is refused. - **Asynchronous agent (Copilot).** Add a `.github/CODEOWNERS` file naming yourself for the protected paths, and turn on branch protection for `main` so that merging requires your review and a passing `r-checks` run: ``` /tests/fixtures/ @your-github-username /tests/make_reference.R @your-github-username /.github/ @your-github-username ``` - **Every route.** Git. `git status --short tests/fixtures` should print nothing for the rest of this block. :::{.callout-warning} **What a deny rule does not cover.** Claude Code's deny rules apply to its built-in file tools, not to commands it runs through the shell. An agent that ran `Rscript tests/make_reference.R` would overwrite your reference without touching an edit tool. That is why git, not the deny rule, is the final check, and why the checklists below ask you to read the agent's command log. ::: You now hold the reference. Pick one path, then rejoin at Step 4. ## Path A: write the function and the test yourself A tidy refactor naturally reaches for the modern `.by` argument. Write this first attempt in `scripts/functions/summary_functions.R`:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: first attempt ---- summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) } ``` :::
Now write the test and run it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_summary_functions.R ---- library(testthat) local_edition(3) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "load_voles.R")) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R")) test_that("summarise_metabolic_rate() reproduces the original summary", { reference <- readRDS(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "metabolic_summary.rds")) expect_equal(summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()), reference, tolerance = 1e-8) }) ``` ::: Run it with `testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_summary_functions.R"))`.
It fails, and not on the numbers. `.by` returns the groups in order of first appearance; the reference, made with `group_by()`, has them sorted. The values are right but the rows are in a different order, and `expect_equal()` reports a mismatch. Add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)` to the end of the pipeline and the test passes. That failure is the lesson in miniature: a change that improved the code altered the output, and the characterisation test caught it. If your test passed first time, the data happen to be stored in sorted order. Check with `load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex)`.
While writing the test, resist one temptation: do not type the expected numbers into the test as literals. A test that compares the function with numbers you transcribed proves nothing about whether the refactor preserved the original computation. The test must *read the `.rds`*. The function you should converge on, with documentation and an argument check:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: refactored ---- #' Summarise post-treatment metabolic rate by treatment arm and sex #' #' @param data A data frame with columns treatment_arm, sex and #' metabolic_rate_post. #' @return A tibble with one row per treatment_arm and sex, sorted by both, #' giving the mean, standard deviation and number of rows. summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { stopifnot(is.data.frame(data)) required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post") missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data)) if (length(missing_cols) > 0) { stop( "`data` is missing required column(s): ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE ) } data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post), n = dplyr::n(), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) |> dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } ``` :::
Finally, make `scripts/02_analysis.R` call the function, so it genuinely replaces the code it came from: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/02_analysis.R: after refactoring ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "01_load_data.R")) source(here("scripts", "functions", "summary_functions.R")) metabolic_summary <- summarise_metabolic_rate(voles) ``` ::: Run the test again; it should still pass. Rejoin at Step 4. ## Path B: a local agent, in two prompts Use this path to let an agent do the work while you verify. Split the job into two prompts, not one. A single prompt that writes both the refactor and the test lets one misunderstanding (about row order, say) shape both files at once, producing a passing test that proves nothing. Separating them stops the test inheriting the refactor's assumptions. **Prompt 1: the refactor only.** ```text Move the computation in scripts/02_analysis.R into a documented function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 02_analysis.R call the new function instead of the inline pipeline. Do not write any tests, and do not touch anything under tests/. ``` Read what it writes. If it uses `.by` without a trailing `arrange()`, leave that for now; the next step will expose it. **Prompt 2: the test only.** ```text Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, read tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds, and compare it with summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) using expect_equal(). Do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not run tests/make_reference.R. I captured that reference myself; a reference you generate proves nothing. ``` Before you trust a passing test, check what the agent wrote and did: 1. The test *reads* `tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds`. It does not hard-code expected numbers. If it does, the check is circular whatever the result. 2. The test calls `summarise_metabolic_rate()`, the function under test, not a reimplementation of the pipeline inside the test. 3. `git status --short tests/fixtures` prints nothing. 4. The agent's command log shows no run of `tests/make_reference.R`. Now run the test yourself. If the function used `.by` without `arrange()`, it fails on row order, not values. Have the agent add `dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex)` and run again. If it passed first time, remove the `arrange()` yourself to see the failure, then restore it. Rejoin at Step 4. ## Path C: an asynchronous agent (Copilot cloud agent) The same work can be handed to an agent that runs remotely while you do something else. It works on a branch in GitHub's infrastructure and returns a pull request. Before you start, check that your Copilot plan includes the coding agent, that `copilot-setup-steps.yml` is on your default branch, and that the CODEOWNERS file and branch protection from Step 0 are in place. Keep the two-step discipline by writing **two issues**, and assign the second only after you have reviewed and merged the first. **Issue 1** ```text Title: Move the metabolic-rate summary into a function Move the summary computation in scripts/02_analysis.R into a documented function summarise_metabolic_rate() in scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, with a roxygen2 block and an argument check. Make 02_analysis.R call it. Acceptance criteria: - Do not add or change anything under tests/, data/ or .github/. - The output must be identical to the current output, including row order and the existing NA value. ``` **Issue 2 (after Issue 1 is merged)** ```text Title: Add a characterisation test for summarise_metabolic_rate() Add tests/test_summary_functions.R. It must call local_edition(3), source scripts/functions/load_voles.R and scripts/functions/summary_functions.R, and compare summarise_metabolic_rate(load_voles()) with tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds using expect_equal(). Acceptance criteria: - Do not create, modify or regenerate anything under tests/fixtures/, and do not run tests/make_reference.R. - Run the tests and report the result in the pull request description. ``` Assign each issue to Copilot. When a pull request arrives: 1. Open **Files changed**. Confirm that only the expected files changed. A change under `tests/fixtures/` or `.github/` should not merge, and CODEOWNERS will in any case require your review for it. 2. Read the test against the four-point checklist in Path B. 3. Check that the `r-checks` run on the pull request passed. 4. Pull the branch and run the test on your own machine. The agent's report that "tests pass" is its claim; your run is the check. If something is wrong, comment on the pull request to ask for a revision, or close it. Nothing reaches `main` until you merge. ## Step 4 (spine): unchanged is not correct Your test passes. The function reproduces the reference exactly, **including the `NA` cell**. The characterisation test has certified that the refactor preserved the original behaviour, and the original behaviour reports a missing mean for one group of animals. Is that the right answer? It depends on what you meant. If you want the mean of the animals that were measured, the original code was wrong all along, and the refactor faithfully preserved the error. A characterisation test cannot tell the difference, because it compares against the past, not against the truth. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Decide, change, and test the change independently :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Decide.** Suppose you conclude that the mean and standard deviation should use the measured animals only. There is a second, quieter problem: `n()` counts rows, including the animal with no measurement, so `n` would no longer match the number of values behind the mean. A summary that reports a mean of 11 animals beside `n = 12` misstates the sample size. **2. Change the function** (by hand or with your agent):
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/summary_functions.R: missing values handled ---- summarise_metabolic_rate <- function(data) { stopifnot(is.data.frame(data)) required <- c("treatment_arm", "sex", "metabolic_rate_post") missing_cols <- setdiff(required, names(data)) if (length(missing_cols) > 0) { stop( "`data` is missing required column(s): ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE ) } data |> dplyr::summarise( mean_rate = mean(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE), sd_rate = stats::sd(metabolic_rate_post, na.rm = TRUE), n_used = sum(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post)), n_missing = sum(is.na(metabolic_rate_post)), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex) ) |> dplyr::arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } ``` :::
**3. Run the characterisation test. It fails, correctly.** The output has changed, and the test exists to tell you so. **4. Add a known-answer test before re-capturing anything.** A known-answer test checks the new behaviour against a result you can compute by hand, independent of any reference file: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # add to tests/test_summary_functions.R ---- test_that("means ignore missing values and n_used counts measured animals", { toy_df <- tibble::tibble( treatment_arm = c("Control", "Control", "Control"), sex = c("F", "F", "F"), metabolic_rate_post = c(10, 14, NA) ) result <- summarise_metabolic_rate(toy_df) expect_equal(result$mean_rate, 12) expect_equal(result$n_used, 2) expect_equal(result$n_missing, 1) }) ``` ::: **5. Only now, re-capture the reference, as a recorded decision.** Re-run `tests/make_reference.R` yourself and commit with a message that states why: ```bash git add tests/fixtures/metabolic_summary.rds scripts/functions/summary_functions.R tests/test_summary_functions.R git commit -m "Exclude missing metabolic rates from mean and SD; report n_used and n_missing" ``` Re-capturing compares the function with itself, so it is acceptable only under three conditions: you decided it, an independent known-answer test checks the new behaviour, and the commit records why. Without those, re-capturing a reference to make a failing test pass is the circular verification this whole block warns against. :::: ::: The general rule: characterisation tests protect behaviour you have already judged correct. Judging it correct is a separate step, and it is yours. ## The environment the test runs in (spine) A characterisation test is only as stable as the environment it runs in. The column types in `load_voles()` handle the finest-grained part. The R version and the package set are handled by two GitHub Actions workflows. `r-checks.yml` is the independent check. It runs the tests from a clean checkout on every push to `main` and on every pull request: ```yaml name: r-checks on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: jobs: tests: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: "4.5.2" # match the R version in renv.lock use-public-rspm: true - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 - name: Run tests run: Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests", stop_on_failure = TRUE)' ``` It is independent of your machine and of the agent's environment, but it is not tamper-proof. A pull request can change the workflow file or the reference it checks against. CODEOWNERS and branch protection (Step 0) are what make a passing run meaningful: you review every change to those paths before it merges. `copilot-setup-steps.yml` builds the environment the Copilot cloud agent works in. Following GitHub's documented pattern: ```yaml name: "Copilot Setup Steps" # Runs when this file changes, so you can see whether setup succeeds, # and can be run by hand from the Actions tab. on: workflow_dispatch: push: paths: - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml pull_request: paths: - .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml jobs: # The job must be called copilot-setup-steps or Copilot will not use it. copilot-setup-steps: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: read steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up R uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 with: r-version: "4.5.2" # match the R version in renv.lock use-public-rspm: true - name: Restore packages from renv.lock uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2 ``` Four requirements, each with a different failure mode: - **The job name must be exactly `copilot-setup-steps`.** If it is not, Copilot ignores the file and works without your packages. That failure is usually loud: the tests error on the first missing function. - **The file must be on the default branch**, or it is not used. - **The runner must be Ubuntu x64 Linux**, the only runner type the cloud agent supports. - **The lockfile must be restored.** If it restores the wrong versions, the failure is quiet: tests run and pass against different package behaviour. The frozen reference then certifies sameness against the wrong baseline. When the agent's test run and the independent `r-checks` run disagree, suspect the environment before you suspect the code. ## From convention to skill The protective sentence in Path B ("do not create, regenerate or modify anything under tests/fixtures/") is a durable convention: it is the same for every refactor. Anything you retype into every prompt is a candidate for a skill. A skill for this workflow would say: capture the reference only if the human has not; never regenerate a fixture; refactor and test in separate steps; compare against the human-held reference. The benefit is that you stop retyping the boundary. The hazard is the same sentence read the other way: once the rule lives in a skill, you no longer see it, and a colleague using your skill may not know that the whole trust argument rests on it. A skill is also only an instruction. The deny rules, CODEOWNERS and git checks in this block hold whether or not the agent reads it. Build the skill only after you have done Path A or B, and keep the "reference stays with the human" clause as a visible line. ## Check your understanding **A characterisation test passes after a refactor. What has it established?**
**Why must the agent never generate the reference file?**
**You have added Edit deny rules for tests/fixtures/ in Claude Code. Which action could still change the reference?**
:::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Instructor notes - Check your copy of `voles_metabolism.csv` before teaching: the `.by` failure in Path A appears only if `load_voles() |> dplyr::distinct(treatment_arm, sex)` is not already in sorted order. If it is sorted, reorder the rows of the file once and commit it before the session. - Confirm that the file contains exactly one missing value in `metabolic_rate_post`, and note which group it falls in, for the Step 4 discussion. - Path C depends on account features. Run it once on a participant-type account before the session. :::
